author: simon-lea
description: In 1832, a novel signed G. Sand struck readers with the truth of its portrait of an unhappily married woman. Behind the man's name was Aurore Dupin, who never hid that she was a woman.

hero.hook: To publish, to observe Paris and to live free, Aurore Dupin borrowed a man's name, a frock coat and a cigar.

blocks.text: George Sand's real name was Amantine Lucile Aurore Dupin de Francueil. Her [[nom de plume]] came from her friend and lover, the novelist [[Jules Sandeau]]. Together they wrote the **1831** novel *Rose et Blanche*, published under the name J. Sand. For the books that followed, written entirely by herself, she kept the name and replaced the J with a G. G for George.

A curious detail: she chose the English spelling, George, rather than the French Georges. It was a way of drawing attention to the name and hinting that all was perhaps not as it seemed. For Sand never hid the fact that her books were written by a woman. Within a year of her first novel, *Indiana*, in **1832**, most of her readers knew that George Sand was female.

*Indiana* was an instant success. The novel tells the story of a young noblewoman trapped in an unhappy marriage and seeking love. She faces infidelity, unrequited love, death and tragedy. Much of Sand's own history can be seen in the book.

blocks.caption: Title page of the first edition of Indiana (Paris, 1832), signed G. Sand.

blocks.text: Yet it was her first novel written alone, and many readers believed it came from the pen of a far more experienced writer. People knew G. Sand was a pseudonym, and speculation about "his" identity was rife. As the author made no attempt to hide, the truth soon spread. Some were not surprised: they had suspected a woman, or at least a female adviser. A man, they thought, could not have written so sensitively about a woman's experience.

George Sand often wore men's clothing when she went out and, even more shocking at the time, she smoked in public. It is tempting to read this as a question of gender identity or a taste for cross-dressing, but things are not so clear cut. In the **19th century**, it was not unheard of for a woman to dress as a man for certain activities, such as horse riding, where feminine clothing was impractical.

blocks.caption: George Sand in a frock coat and trousers, cigar in hand: caricature by Alcide Lorentz, 1842.

blocks.text: Above all, a woman on her own rarely moved freely about town. To go out and observe life, the raw material of her novels, without drawing attention, men's clothes were all but essential. Her love life was complicated. She was bisexual, but preferred the company of men. One of her most famous female lovers was the actress [[Marie Dorval]], to whom she devoted an entire chapter of her autobiography.

Sand's work was very well received, by the public and by fellow writers and artists alike. [[Gustave Flaubert]], the author of *Madame Bovary* and *Sentimental Education*, was particularly taken with her. In his letters he called her "Chère Maître": "chère" in the feminine, "maître" in the masculine. Proust mentions her in *In Search of Lost Time*, Dostoevsky in *Notes from Underground*. At her funeral, it was **Victor Hugo** who gave the eulogy.

blocks.caption: Chopin at the piano and George Sand listening: unfinished double portrait by Eugène Delacroix, 1838.

blocks.text: For almost **ten years**, Sand shared a passionate and stormy relationship with the composer [[Frédéric Chopin]]. The parting was bitter. Sand settled the score in her own way: in **1846**, in her novel *Lucrezia Floriani*, she gave the weak and sickly character of Karol the features of Chopin.

George Sand also wrote political essays and pamphlets. Her life spanned the great upheavals of France: the revolution of **1848**, then the rise and fall of the [[Paris Commune]] in **1871**. She leaned toward socialism and was passionate about human freedom, especially the freedom of women to take control of their own lives. Many people still draw inspiration from her ideas today.
Napoleon was in power when she was born. He left for his first exile when she was ten, and returned a year later for the [[Hundred Days]].

One paradox remains. George Sand is still a popular and greatly admired writer, in France and abroad. But in the English-speaking world she is best known for the life she lived, whereas in the French-speaking world she is read first of all for her books.
Aurore Dupin took a man's name, a frock coat and a cigar not to hide, but to publish, to observe the world and to live free, without ever denying that she was a woman.

sources.text: M. Reid, George Sand, Penn State University Press, 2018, p. 63.
